draft.title: Inequality signs and number lines
card: The sign \(<\) means less than and \(>\) means greater than. So \(x < 5\) means \(x\) is any number below 5.
The sign \(\le\) means less than or equal to and \(\ge\) means greater than or equal to. "At least" means \(\ge\) and "at most" means \(\le\).
On a number line, draw an open circle when the number itself is not included (\(<\) or \(>\)). Draw a closed circle when it is included (\(\le\) or \(\ge\)). Then shade towards the values that work.
Example: \(x > 3\) has an open circle at 3, because 3 does not work, and is shaded to the right.

4.alt: A number line from \(-1\) to 8. An open circle at 3 with a line shaded to the right, showing \(x > 3\).

draft.remember: Open circle: the number is left out. Closed circle: the number is in. Shade the side that works.

a.q: Which description matches \(x \le 2\) on a number line?
opts: Closed circle at 2, shaded to the left
Open circle at 2, shaded to the left
Closed circle at 2, shaded to the right
Open circle at 2, shaded to the right
a.why: The sign \(\le\) includes 2, so the circle is closed. Values less than 2 are to the left, so the shading goes left. An open circle would leave 2 out, which suits only \(x < 2\).
a.clue: Does 2 itself work, and are the other answers bigger or smaller?

b.q: A ride at a Ballarat fun park needs riders to be at least 120 cm tall. Which inequality shows the height \(h\) that is allowed?
b.why: At least 120 cm means 120 cm or taller, so 120 is included and the sign is \(\ge\). The sign \(>\) is tempting, but it would leave out a rider who is exactly 120 cm.
b.clue: Can a rider who is exactly 120 cm go on?

a.best: Closed circle at 2, shaded to the left

problems.detail: In the example graph, the shaded line runs only from 3 to 7.5 and ends there, with no arrow. A student could read this as the solution stopping before 8, when x > 3 goes on forever. The shading should end in an arrow at the right edge.
